content.text: In the previous lesson on static electricity, we studied charges that accumulate and remain stationary on the surface of objects. Now we turn our attention to charges in motion —
. Electric current is the foundation of almost all modern technology: from the lights in your home, to the phone in your pocket, to the machines in hospitals and factories.

Understanding what current is, how it relates to charge, and how we measure it is essential before we can analyse circuits and electrical devices. In this lesson, we will define electric current, explore the relationship between current and charge, distinguish between conventional current and electron flow, and learn how to measure current in a circuit.

When a conducting wire is connected to a source of electrical energy (such as a battery), the free electrons in the wire are pushed in a particular direction. This orderly flow of electrons through the conductor constitutes an electric current.
Without a complete circuit (a closed loop), current cannot flow. If there is a break anywhere in the circuit — such as an open switch — the flow of charge stops.

In metallic conductors (such as copper wire), the charge carriers are

(also called conduction electrons or delocalised electrons). These electrons are not bound to any particular atom and are free to drift through the metal lattice when a potential difference is applied.

In a metal at room temperature, even without a battery connected, the free electrons are in constant random motion, moving in all directions at very high speeds. However, this random motion does not produce a net current because the electrons move equally in all directions, so the overall flow in any particular direction is zero.

When a battery or other source of EMF is connected, an electric field is established in the wire. This field exerts a force on the free electrons, causing them to drift slowly in one direction (from the negative terminal of the battery towards the positive terminal). This slow, directed movement is called
, and it is typically very small — on the order of millimetres per second, even though the electrons' random speeds are much higher.

Despite the slow drift velocity, electrical signals travel through circuits at nearly the speed of light. This is because when the electric field is established, it affects all the free electrons in the wire almost simultaneously, much like pushing one end of a long tube filled with marbles causes the marble at the other end to move almost immediately.

Both descriptions are valid and give correct results when used consistently. By convention, physicists and engineers continue to use conventional current direction in circuit diagrams, equations, and analysis. All rules (such as Fleming's rules) are based on the conventional current direction.

On a current-time graph, DC appears as a straight horizontal line (for steady DC) at a constant value above or below zero.

In the UK, the mains electricity supply is AC with a frequency of 50 Hz (50 cycles per second). In some other countries (such as the USA), the mains frequency is 60 Hz.
On a current-time graph, AC appears as a
(a smooth, repeating S-shaped curve) oscillating above and below zero.
Key differences between AC and DC:

| Property | DC | AC |
|---|---|---|
| Direction of flow | One direction only | Reverses direction periodically |
| Source | Battery, solar cell | Generator, mains supply |
| Graph shape | Horizontal line | Sinusoidal wave |
| Transmission | Loses more energy over long distances | Can be transmitted efficiently using transformers |
| Frequency | Zero (no oscillation) | Typically 50 Hz or 60 Hz |
AC has a major advantage for power transmission: it can be easily stepped up to high voltage (and low current) using
for efficient long-distance transmission, and then stepped down again for safe use in homes and businesses. DC cannot be transformed in this way (without first converting it to AC).

"Current is used up as it goes around a circuit."
This is one of the most persistent misconceptions in physics. Current is
used up. The same current flows into and out of each component in a series circuit. What is "used up" (or more accurately, transferred) is
, not charge. The charges (electrons) circulate continuously around the circuit.
"Current flows from positive to negative because positive charges move."

In metallic conductors, it is the negatively charged electrons that actually move, and they flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. Conventional current direction (positive to negative) is a historical convention, not a description of what physically moves in a metal.
The current in a circuit depends on both the EMF (voltage) of the battery

the total resistance of the circuit. A bigger battery (higher EMF) will produce more current only if the resistance stays the same. If you connect a high-EMF battery to a high-resistance circuit, the current could still be small.
"Electrons travel at the speed of light through a wire."
The drift velocity of electrons is actually very slow (typically less than 1 mm/s). What travels at nearly the speed of light is the
(the signal), which pushes all the electrons in the wire almost simultaneously.

with the component. Connecting it in parallel would short-circuit the component and could damage the ammeter due to excessive current.
"AC and DC only differ in direction."

While the defining difference is that AC reverses direction and DC does not, they also differ in how they are generated, transmitted, and used. AC can be efficiently transformed to different voltages using transformers, which is crucial for power distribution.
